The stressed syllable is usually lengthened, and the pre-stressed syllable tends to be a higher pitch in words of three or more syllables. Stress falls on the penultimate syllable, except where this is a high vowel, /u/ or /i/ preceded by the lower vowel, /o/ or /e/ respectively, where there is a widespread tendency for the penultimate syllable to be omitted altogether." p.21, sec. 8: "In words of four or more syllables, every second preceding syllable has a secondary stress with one exception: the secondary stress always falls on the first syllable to be reduplicated even though the primary stress is 3 syllables away"

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog (StressTyp2) records penult primary with alternating secondary stresses leftward (stress placement coded per word length as 10 010 1010 01010 101010 (1 = a stressed syllable)). Ezard & Ezard 1974 state exactly this (penultimate primary; secondary on every second preceding syllable) and add detail the catalog lacks: the reduplication exception for secondary stress, the penult-vowel elision cases (o+u, e+i), final /mu/ -> [m] leaving stress phonetically final, and the phonetic correlates (length on the stressed syllable, raised pitch on the pre-tonic). Dialect described: Diwinai (central dialect).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is fixed on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word (pitch and length non-phonemic; stressed syllable lengthened, pre-stress syllable higher-pitched). Examples: /keduluma/ [kedu'lumʌ] 'woman', /lalawa/ [la'lawʌ], /kabudela/ [kabu'dela]. Secondary stress falls on every second syllable to the left of the primary stress in words of four or more syllables (/anugonugotuhu/ [a'nugo'nugo"tuhu]).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Alternating: every second syllable preceding the primary (penult) stress carries secondary stress in words of 4+ syllables; exception: in reduplications the secondary stress always falls on the first syllable of the reduplicated material even when the primary stress is three syllables away (/idewadewa/ [i'dewa''dewʌ], /idewadewaya/ [i'dewade''waya]).
new_statements.exceptions: (1) When the penult is a high vowel /u/ or /i/ preceded by /o/ or /e/ respectively, the penultimate syllable tends to be dropped, giving surface variants (/ginouli/ [gi'nouli] ~ [gi'noli], /baneina/ [ba'neinʌ] ~ [ba'nenʌ]). (2) Sec. 3.2.2(b), p.7: word-final /mu/ loses its /u/ phonetically and 'almost all words with [m] final retain the stress on the final vowel' (/aipomu/ [ai'pom] 'evening', /pomupamu/ [pom'pam]) -- i.e. stress stays on the phonemic penult, which is then phonetically final. (3) Reduplication overrides the alternating count for secondary stress. (4) A very few monosyllabic words exist (footnote p.19). Phrase level (sec. 9, p.22): the nuclear syllable of the last word in the phonological phrase is loudest, longest and lowest in pitch; question vs statement phrases differ in pitch contour.
new_statements.identity_note: Ezard & Ezard 1974 explicitly describe the Diwinai (Divinai) dialect, 'a central dialect, midway between East Cape and Rabe dialects', data collected during 4 months' residence at Divinai in 1974 (Introduction, printed p.2); they note Sideia and Basilaki islands speak a more divergent dialect of the Tawala chain.

audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed penultimate primary stress with leftward alternating secondary stress, stress placement coded per word length as 10 010 1010 01010 (1 = a stressed syllable)) rests on the standard reference grammar, Ezard 1997 PL C-137 section 4.5, which we hold with a clean text; every quoted fragment was confirmed verbatim on printed pp.44-45 (pp.60-61). The secondary-stress rule in the grammar ('first of every two syllables prior to the primary-stressed syllable, counting leftward') matches the coded rule string (e.g. 5 syllables -> 01010). Glottolog's bibliography offers nothing better: all descriptive works are Ezard's, and the 1997 volume is the published form of the 1990/91 dissertation that StressTyp2 cites. sources.quote: Stress in Tawala is predictable, occurring on the penultimate (second to last) syllable. Stress includes not only increased volume but also increased length and a rise in pitch. [...] There is a distinction between primary stress (penultimate) and secondary stress (word or root initial etc.), the latter showing little increase in length. [...] The phonological word in Tawala is a group of syllables attached to a primary stress. The word nucleus is marked by a primary-stressed syllable and it has optional prenuclear margins and a single postnuclear margin. Hence stress is placed on the penultimate syllable: [ev n] 'evev. [...] Secondary stress is applied (counting leftward) to the first of every two syllables prior to the primary-stressed syllable, subject to the rule: ("evev)n 'evev. [...] Secondary stress always applies to the beginning of a reduplicated form. This rule overrides the previous rule. [...] When the syllable to be stressed (primary or secondary) is the second vowel in a vv sequence, if it is a higher vowel than the preceding one the stress moves to the preceding syllable and the double vowel becomes a glide.

The phonology section (0.3, p. 8) gives only a 20-phoneme inventory for the Diwinai dialect plus three notes (s/t distinction, negligible allophony, the single closed-syllable type) and refers phonological justification to Ezard, B. & J. 1974 'Tawala Phonology' (unpublished MS). No statement of word stress, accent, weight, secondary stress or tone anywhere; no accent marks in the text.
